items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that a statement [MATH: \beta] follows from statements [MATH: \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] if [MATH: \beta] is true whenever all of [MATH: \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] are true. This is called a logical inference.

Content:
Let's consider another logical inference rule known as disjunctive syllogism (disjunction elimination or simply elimination). We can state this rule as follows:

Content:
[MATH: P∨Q; ¬P; ∴Q]

Content:
This rule reads as follows:

Content:
> We have [MATH: P \lor Q] and [MATH: \lnot P.] Therefore, [MATH: Q.]

Content:
To check that the rule is valid, we can use a truth table:

Content:
| | | | Premise 1 | Premise 2 | Conclusion |
| [MATH: P] | [MATH: Q] | | [MATH: P \lor Q] | [MATH: \lnot P] | [MATH: Q] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{red} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |

Content:
Both [MATH: P \lor Q] and [MATH: \lnot P] have the truth value [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] (true) only in the third row of the table. For this row, [MATH: Q] is also [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] (true). So, according to the definition, we have a logical inference.

Content:
Since disjunction is commutative and the order of the premises does not matter, we have the following variants of the rule:

Content:
[MATH: P∨Q; ¬P; ∴Q]

According to the disjunctive syllogism inference rule, what is missing from the series of statements below?

[MATH: [math]x[/math] is divisible by [math]3[/math] or [math]x[/math] is prime; [math]x[/math] is not prime; [m a t h] x [/ m a t h] i s d i v i s i b l e b y [m a t h] 3 [/ m a t h].]

According to the disjunctive syllogism inference rule, what is missing from the series of statements below?

[MATH: [math]x[/math] is divisible by [math]3[/math] or [math]x[/math] is prime; [math]x[/math] is not prime; [m a t h] x [/ m a t h] i s d i v i s i b l e b y [m a t h] 3 [/ m a t h].]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The logical inference rule of disjunctive syllogism asserts that if [MATH: P] or [MATH: Q] is true, yet [MATH: P] is false, then [MATH: Q] must be true.

Let's denote:

  • [MATH: D(x):] [MATH: x] is divisible by [MATH: 3]

  • [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is prime

Then, using our disjunctive syllogism inference rule, we obtain the following:

[MATH: D∨P; ¬P; ∴D]

Therefore, we have:

[MATH: [math]x[/math] divisible by [math]3[/math] or [math]x[/math] is prime; [math]x[/math] is not prime; ∴[math]x[/math] is divisible by [math]3[/math]]

[MATH: If [math]x[/math] is positive, then [math]2x[/math] is positive; If [math]2x[/math] is positive, then [math]2x+1[/math] is positive; ∴A A A A A A A A A A A]

Content:
The logical inference rule of transitivity of implication asserts that if [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q] is true, and [MATH: Q] implies [MATH: R] is true, then [MATH: P] implies [MATH: R] must be true.

Content:
Let's denote:

Content:
- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is positive
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: 2x] is positive
- [MATH: R(x):] [MATH: 2x+1] is positive

Content:
Then, using the transitivity of implication rule, we obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; Q⇒R; ∴P⇒R]

Content:
Therefore, we have:

Content:
[MATH: If [math]x[/math] is positive, then [math]2x[/math] is positive; If [math]2x[/math] is positive, then [math]2x+1[/math] is positive; ∴If [math]x[/math] is positive, then [math]2x+1[/math] is positive]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that a statement [MATH: \beta] follows from statements [MATH: \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] if [MATH: \beta] is true whenever all of [MATH: \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n] are true. This is called a logical inference.

Content:
Let's consider another logical inference rule known as disjunctive syllogism (disjunction elimination or simply elimination). We can state this rule as follows:

Content:
[MATH: P∨Q; ¬P; ∴Q]

Content:
This rule reads as follows:

Content:
> We have [MATH: P \lor Q] and [MATH: \lnot P.] Therefore, [MATH: Q.]

Content:
To check that the rule is valid, we can use a truth table:

Content:
| | | | Premise 1 | Premise 2 | Conclusion |
| [MATH: P] | [MATH: Q] | | [MATH: P \lor Q] | [MATH: \lnot P] | [MATH: Q] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{red} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |

Content:
Both [MATH: P \lor Q] and [MATH: \lnot P] have the truth value [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] (true) only in the third row of the table. For this row, [MATH: Q] is also [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] (true). So, according to the definition, we have a logical inference.

Content:
Since disjunction is commutative and the order of the premises does not matter, we have the following variants of the rule:

Content:
[MATH: P∨Q; ¬P; ∴Q]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Concrete Example

Content:
Let's complete the following logical inference:

Content:
[MATH: [math]x[/math] is positive or [math]x[/math] is less than [math]-1[/math]; [math]x[/math] is not positive; ∴A A A A A A A A A A A]

Content:
The logical inference rule of disjunctive syllogism asserts that if [MATH: P] or [MATH: Q] is true, yet [MATH: P] is false, then [MATH: Q] must be true.

Content:
Let's denote:

Content:
- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is positive
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: x] is less than [MATH: -1]

Content:
Then, using the disjunctive syllogism rule, we obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: P∨Q; ¬P; ∴Q]

Content:
Therefore, we have:

Content:
[MATH: [math]x[/math] is positive or [math]x[/math] is less than [math]-1[/math]; [math]x[/math] is not positive; ∴[math]x[/math] is less than [math]-1[/math]]

---

EXPLANATION

In the case above, the disjunctive syllogism inference rule can be written as follows:

[MATH: ¬K; K∨M; ∴M]

Therefore, the missing part is [MATH: M.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Transitivity of Implication

Content:
Another important rule of logical inference is called transitivity of implication (chain argument or hypothetical syllogism):

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; Q⇒R; ∴P⇒R]

Content:
This rule is read as follows:

Content:
> We have [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: Q \Rightarrow R.] Therefore, [MATH: P \Rightarrow R.]

| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] | [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] | [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] | [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] | [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | | [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] | [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] | [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | | [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] | [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] | [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] |

Content:
Both [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] and [MATH: Q \Rightarrow R] have the truth value [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathrm{T}}] (true) in the first, fifth, seventh, and eighth rows of the table only. For these rows, [MATH: P \Rightarrow R] also has the truth value [MATH: {\color{red}\mathrm{T}}] (true). So, according to the definition, we have a logical inference.

Content:
Since the order of the premises does not matter, we have the following variants of the rule:

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q; Q⇒R; ∴P⇒R]
